statement: In the one study that scanned people before they had ever used ecstasy and again afterwards, starting to use it in small amounts did not change serotonin transporter binding. 188 people who had never used ecstasy were imaged; about 17 months later, 59 who had begun using (mean 6.0 tablets, median 2; last tablet a mean of 18.7 weeks earlier) and 56 matched people who had not were imaged again. Transporter binding with [123I]beta-CIT did not differ at follow-up in any region (midbrain 0.036, 95% CI -0.068 to 0.140; thalamus -0.001, -0.077 to 0.076; frontal -0.003, -0.036 to 0.31 as printed; occipital -0.018, -0.051 to 0.015; temporal -0.009, -0.053 to 0.35 as printed, the last two upper limits almost certainly misprints for 0.031 and 0.035), nor did brain metabolites, and a voxel-by-voxel analysis found nothing. Four smaller differences did appear, each under 5% and within the normal range of the age group: lower fractional anisotropy in thalamus and frontoparietal white matter, higher anisotropy in globus pallidus, a higher apparent diffusion coefficient in thalamus, and lower relative cerebral blood volume in globus pallidus and putamen. The two groups did not differ on any imaging measure, substance use or transporter genotype before anyone had used ecstasy, which is the one direct check on the objection that differences seen in people who use ecstasy were there beforehand. The transporter result cannot be read as showing that heavier use leaves binding unchanged: the doses were very low, the tracer is not selective for the serotonin transporter and the authors judge it too insensitive for small changes, 32 comparisons were made without correction, and the group that started also increased its use of alcohol, cannabis, amphetamine and cocaine. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: One Dutch study scanned young people before they had ever taken ecstasy, then again about a year and a half later. By then some had started, but most had taken only one or two pills. Their serotonin marker had not changed, and nor had the chemical measures. A few small differences showed up in other brain measures, all under 5%. Before anyone had used ecstasy the two groups' scans looked the same, which matters because people often ask whether the differences seen later were there all along. The doses here were tiny and the scan used an older, less exact marker, so this says nothing about heavier use.
population: Young adults in the Netherlands who had never used ecstasy and were judged likely to start
exposure: Starting to use ecstasy, a median of 2 tablets over about 17 months
comparator: The same people before any use, and matched people from the same cohort who did not start
outcome: Serotonin transporter binding with [123I]beta-CIT SPECT, brain metabolites, diffusion measures and cerebral blood volume
magnitude: Transporter binding at follow-up, adjusted for baseline (regression coefficients, 95% CI): midbrain 0.036 (-0.068 to 0.140), thalamus -0.001 (-0.077 to 0.076), frontal grey matter -0.003 (-0.036 to 0.31 as printed), occipital -0.018 (-0.051 to 0.015), temporal -0.009 (-0.053 to 0.35 as printed; the frontal and temporal upper limits appear to be misprints for 0.031 and 0.035). The binding ratios themselves are 1.1 to 1.3 in midbrain and thalamus but 0.01 to 0.05 in cortical grey matter, so the cortical intervals, although narrow in absolute units, do not exclude a large proportional change. Differences that did appear were under 5%: fractional anisotropy -8.16 (-15.30 to -1.02) in thalamus and -8.23 (-14.35 to -2.10) in frontoparietal white matter, +23.19 (3.65 to 42.73) in globus pallidus (all x1000); apparent diffusion coefficient +3.68 (0.67 to 6.69) x10-5 mm2/s in thalamus; relative cerebral blood volume -0.083 (-0.154 to -0.012) in globus pallidus and -0.058 (-0.110 to -0.006) in putamen.

evidence.locator: Table 1 (p. 2940, exposure); Table 2, SPECT and 1H-MRS rows (p. 2941)
evidence.extracted: Prospective cohort: 59 people who started using ecstasy (mean 6.0 tablets, median 2) and 56 who did not, imaged before any use and about 17 months later. Transporter binding at follow-up, adjusted for baseline: midbrain 0.036 (95% CI -0.068 to 0.140), thalamus -0.001 (-0.077 to 0.076), frontal grey matter -0.003 (-0.036 to 0.31 as printed), occipital -0.018 (-0.051 to 0.015), temporal -0.009 (-0.053 to 0.35 as printed; the frontal and temporal upper limits are almost certainly misprints for 0.031 and 0.035, checked on the rendered page). All nine metabolite ratios were also unchanged.

evidence.locator: Results, 'Brain imaging', 3rd paragraph (p. 2939); Table 2, DTI and PWI rows (p. 2941); Figure 2 (p. 2942)
evidence.extracted: Differences that did appear, all under 5% and after adjustment for sex, baseline verbal IQ, age, education and use of alcohol, cannabis, amphetamines, cocaine and tobacco: fractional anisotropy lower in thalamus (-8.16, 95% CI -15.30 to -1.02, x1000) and frontoparietal white matter (-8.23, -14.35 to -2.10) and higher in globus pallidus (+23.19, 3.65 to 42.73); apparent diffusion coefficient higher in thalamus (+3.68, 0.67 to 6.69); relative cerebral blood volume lower in globus pallidus (-0.083, -0.154 to -0.012) and putamen (-0.058, -0.110 to -0.006). Part of each difference comes from change in the group that did not start.

evidence.locator: Results, 'Characteristics of the sample and substance use' (p. 2939); Table 1 (p. 2940); Table 2, baseline columns (p. 2941)
evidence.extracted: Before anyone had used ecstasy the two groups did not differ on any imaging parameter, on substance use or on serotonin-transporter genotype. Over follow-up the group that started increased its use of alcohol (p=0.036), cannabis (p=0.029), amphetamines (p=0.047) and cocaine (p=0.017) more than the other group, and their interval between sessions was shorter (15.9 vs 18.3 months, p=0.024).

The authors state that statistical power may have been insufficient for SPECT and spectroscopy given the low doses, that the tracer may be too insensitive to detect mild changes (animal work shows it underestimates MDMA-induced transporter loss), that no correction for multiple comparisons was applied in order to limit false negatives, and that the observed effects may be reversible adaptations rather than permanent neurotoxicity.

evidence.locator: Results › Neuropsychological Testing, 2nd paragraph (p. 731); Comment, 1st paragraph (p. 732)
evidence.extracted: In the same cohort, verbal learning improved less in those who had started using ecstasy (immediate recall +0.86 against +3.90 words; adjusted difference 2.23, 95% CI 0.17 to 4.29, p=0.03), while overall test performance in both groups stayed within the normal range for the general population.

evidence.locator: Table 4, de Win et al. (2008a) row; Discussion, 'Serotonin transporter', 1st paragraph
evidence.extracted: The review lists this cohort among the two of 16 human transporter studies that did not find a significant reduction, and reports for it an occipital change of -40% computed from binding ratios of 0.05 against 0.03; the review does not flag that these near-zero values make the percentage meaningless, although it makes that point about another study's figures.

risk_of_bias.note: Not randomized: people chose whether to start, and those who did also increased their use of alcohol, cannabis, amphetamine and cocaine and were re-tested sooner. Exposure is self-reported and tablet content unverified. The pre-use measurement removes most of the usual confounding, which is why only one level is taken.

inconsistency.note: A single cohort; nothing to compare it with, since no other prospective imaging study exists.

indirectness.note: The exposure is a median of 2 tablets, far below that of the people in the cross-sectional studies, and the tracer is not selective for the serotonin transporter and is judged by the authors too insensitive for small changes; so this bears only indirectly on what ordinary or heavy use does.

imprecision.note: Not downgraded again: the intervals are reported and the claim states what they do and do not exclude. In cortical regions the binding ratios are near zero, so the intervals are narrow in absolute units but wide in proportion.

dose_response.note: Not applied: no dose-response was found, and the range of use was too narrow to test one.

grade.reasoning: Observational evidence starts low, downgraded for risk of bias (self-selected starters with more other drug use and a shorter interval between sessions) and indirectness (a median of 2 tablets, measured with a tracer the authors call too insensitive). The claim is worded as no detectable change at this exposure and states the limits that stop it being read as no change at any exposure.

verification.flag_note: Anchors are ai-located and need a second reader. The companion paper on the thalamus from the same cohort (de Win et al., Br J Psychiatry 2008;193:289-296, doi 10.1192/bjp.bp.106.035089) has not been read and has no reference record; it reports the same cohort's thalamic findings and should be added before this claim is shown.

changelog.change: Drafted (AI reader 45, MDMA batch 5a) from the one prospective imaging cohort, read in full, with its cognitive companion paper and the review as qualifying anchors.
